questions_asked: When a few self-driving cars join a normal highway, what is the single most important way they help traffic move better?
If most cars on a road are self-driving, roughly how much less space between cars can they safely keep than human drivers?
By how much would you need to see peak-hour congestion drop before recommending dedicated self-driving car lanes?
expert_answers:
The single most important effect is smoothing: a self-driving car with good sensors and short reaction time can follow the car ahead at a smaller, steadier gap and damp the stop-and-go waves that human drivers amplify. That reduces the "phantom" braking cascades that cause most congestion at high density, so throughput rises even at low penetration.

This only holds if the automated car's car-following is stable and it can actually see far enough ahead; if it instead mimics human reaction times or drives conservatively with large gaps, the benefit largely disappears.

At high automation penetration, cooperative self-driving cars can safely run at roughly **one-third to one-half** the headway (time gap) of human drivers — i.e., they can keep about **50–70% less space** between cars than a human-driven stream at the same speed.

Concretely: human drivers at highway speed typically maintain ~1.5–2 s headway; cooperative automated cars with short reaction times and vehicle-to-vehicle coordination can plausibly run ~0.5–1 s. That translates to roughly **2–3× higher lane throughput** in the ideal case.

This is an empirical/engineering judgment, not a precise figure. It assumes stable car-following, reliable sensing, and coordination; without those, the reduction shrinks toward zero.

A dedicated-lane recommendation needs a **large, durable** peak-hour improvement — not a marginal one. As a rule of thumb, I would want to see peak-hour delay or travel time fall by roughly **20–30% or more** on the affected corridor, and hold up across the 10%→50%→90% penetration range, before recommending lane dedication.

The reason for a high bar: dedicating a lane removes capacity from the general-purpose traffic, so the gain must clearly exceed that loss. If the improvement is only a few percent, or appears only at high penetration, the lane is more likely to worsen overall congestion than relieve it.

This is an empirical judgment, not a precise threshold; the exact figure depends on how much the dedicated lane actually raises throughput versus how much general capacity it takes away.
